newsitem.title: UK: City punters offer Conservatives crumb of comfort.
newsitem.headline: City punters offer Conservatives crumb of comfort.

text.p: Opinion polls may predict doom and gloom for the Conservatives in Britain's election, but traders in the City of London offer the ruling party a crumb of comfort.
London's traditionally Conservative-supporting financial district is betting that Labour's expected victory on May 1 will be less sensational than the surveys suggest.
"Everybody is buying the Conservatives and selling Labour," said Patrick Jay, head of the sports desk -- which covers political betting -- at financial bookmaker IG Index.

"Spread betting" is all the rage at the financial bookies. City Index, for example, quotes Labour's parliamentary majority at a bid/offer spread of 78-88 seats, meaning a punter who expects Labour's majority to top that can go 'long' at 88.

"As soon as the election was announced, we were quoting (a Labour majority of) around 90-100. That got sold all the way back to about 70-80 and it's now pulling up again," said Paul Barnett, political market maker at City Index.
The Conservatives announced the May 1 election date on March 17, hoping a long campaign would allow it to claw back Labour's hefty opinion poll lead.
That triggered big buying of the Conservatives and selling of Labour at the start of the election campaign, said Barnett.
"But we're now starting to see some buyers for the Labour party as the Conservatives fail to make any great headway in the polls," he said.
City Index is currently quoting the number of seats Labour will win at 368-374, with the Conservatives at 238-244. At IG Index, Labour is on 367-373 and Conservative 239-245.

The latest Gallup snapshot poll of 1,000 voters for Friday's Daily Telegraph showed 52 percent favouring Labour. The Conservatives lagged behind on 31 percent and the centrist Liberal Democrats accounted for 11 percent.

Gallup's findings suggest the Conservatives will win just 171 seats, giving Labour 443 and its largest overall majority ever of 227.A party needs 330 seats for an overall majority in the 659-seat House of Commons.
